questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Planning services from an undercounted population
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an undercounted population distorts service planning
questions.stem: Translator's note A4: The passage says the census recorded 61,000 residents in the district, so clarify what an undercount does to the design of water and waste services.

options.text: Service capacity is planned for too few people, so the network is undersized from the start
Nothing changes, because service planning only depends on the number of registered households
options.misconception: assumes household counts can stand in for population counts

options.text: An undercount raises revenue, because fewer residents are counted for taxation
options.misconception: claims an undercount increases the taxable base

options.text: The effect disappears once the first census is followed by a second one
options.misconception: assumes a later count repairs planning errors on the first

questions.explanation: Planning capacity from an undercount sets networks for too few residents, and the shortfall appears later as pressure on supply. A second count documents the error but does not undo the capacity.
questions.hint: Ask what the planning was based on.

questions.topic: Rate at which an enumeration missed residents
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a coverage rate from an enumeration
questions.stem: Translator's note B12: The passage reports that the enumeration reached 83 per cent of expected residents, and the note must convey what that rate means.

options.text: The rate shows the enumeration was thorough, since most residents were reached
options.misconception: treats a high coverage rate as proof of a flawless count

options.text: Roughly one resident in six was not counted, so the true population is above the recorded figure
The recorded population is exactly 83 per cent of the true one
options.misconception: reads coverage as the share of the true population recorded

options.text: Seventeen per cent of residents were confirmed as absent from the district
options.misconception: confuses an undercount rate with a rate of residents leaving

questions.explanation: An 83 per cent coverage rate implies the recorded figure is roughly a sixth short of the true population. It measures completeness of the count, not how accurate the list is.
questions.hint: Convert the coverage rate into a shortfall.

questions.topic: Remittances and rural household spending
questions.learningObjective: Explain how remittance income changes rural household spending
questions.stem: Gloss entry 21: The passage describes money sent home by migrants and asks how the translator should convey its effect on rural household spending.

options.text: Remittances reduce rural spending, because households send most of what they receive straight back
options.misconception: assumes transferred income is returned, not spent locally

options.text: Remittances raise rural spending only when the village has no market nearby
options.misconception: links spending effects to market access without any evidence

options.text: Remittances relax the household budget, allowing spending on education, inputs and health
Remittances leave rural spending unchanged, since the money is spent in the city where it is earned
options.misconception: assumes money sent home is spent where it is earned

questions.explanation: Money arriving from outside relaxes the binding constraint on rural households, which is income, so spending rises on inputs, health and schooling. It is spent locally.
questions.hint: Consider what income was the constraint before.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Movement from city centre to its own region
questions.learningObjective: Set out what out-migration from a city centre changes
questions.stem: Term note 18: The source passage describes residents moving out of the historic core into the surrounding region, and the note must set out what that shift changes.

answer.exemplar: Out-migration from the core changes who uses central assets and who pays for them. The core keeps a concentration of infrastructure sized for a larger population, while the receiving region has to extend its own networks for new households. Tax bases move at different speeds from demand, so the two areas experience the same shift in opposite directions and no single adjustment fixes both.

questions.explanation: Moving residents redraws demand while infrastructure stays fixed, so the core carries costs for fewer users and the region pays to extend networks. Each area sees the opposite effect.
questions.hint: Ask who keeps using the old assets.

questions.stem: Translator's note C7: A road project is expected to raise land values along it by 900 per cent, and the note must calculate the new value of a plot priced at 12,000.
questions.explanation: A rise of 900 per cent means the value multiplies by ten, so a plot at 12,000 becomes 120,000. The increase is 108,000, and capturing part of it repays the project.
questions.hint: Turn the percentage rise into a multiplier.

questions.topic: Charging for peak road use
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a peak-hour road charge is designed to achieve

stimulus.body: A scheme charges higher tolls between 7 and 9 on weekdays and lower rates outside those hours. Vehicles that never travel in the peak hours receive a discount, and the revenue funds road maintenance on the routes used in peak times.

questions.stem: Translator's note D30: The passage describes a peak-hour toll with a discount for off-peak users, and the note must convey what the scheme is designed to achieve.

options.text: The toll is designed to raise revenue from all drivers regardless of when they travel
options.misconception: ignores the time and route targeting built into the pricing

options.text: The discount for off-peak drivers is intended to reduce driving at all hours
options.misconception: mistakes a peak-hour scheme for a general cut in driving

options.text: Peak pricing works by discouraging the journeys that cause the least damage
options.misconception: assumes the scheme targets the journeys with least impact

options.text: The charge puts price on the hours and routes where congestion is worst

questions.explanation: Pricing peaks and congested routes targets the congestion and directs revenue towards the wear peak use causes. Off-peak discounts protect occasional users rather than reducing driving generally.
questions.hint: Ask what the pricing is aimed at.

options.text: A substantial share of households must still carry and pay for the water they use
The remaining two thirds have reliable access, so water access is solved
options.misconception: treats two thirds with access as proof the problem is closed

options.text: Thirty-four per cent of households use no water at all during the dry season
options.misconception: confuses having no connection with having no water at all

options.text: Standpipes are illegal in the area, so the figure reflects regulation
options.misconception: invokes a regulatory ban not mentioned in the passage

questions.explanation: Without a connection or a standpipe, households buy and carry water themselves, at a cost in money and time. Two thirds with access still leaves a large minority without reliable supply.

questions.learningObjective: Convey how a documentary condition affects who receives a service
questions.stem: Translator's note E5: The passage says proof of residence is required before a household receives a water connection, and the note must convey the policy's effect.

options.text: Requiring documents raises the number of connections recorded in the system
options.misconception: confuses a gatekeeping rule with an expansion of coverage

options.text: Households without documents cannot obtain the service, whatever their need
Households without documents pay a higher fee but still receive the connection
options.misconception: confuses a documentary barrier with a pricing barrier

options.text: Proof of residence is an optional formality that most households already satisfy
options.misconception: assumes a documentary requirement does not exclude anyone

questions.explanation: A documentary condition is a gate: households lacking papers are refused the service regardless of need, so the policy shapes who appears in the records. How many hold papers is a separate question.

questions.topic: Two readings of urban informality
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the two senses of informality used in the source
questions.stem: Sense note 12: The source uses the same word for both unlicensed roadside trade and self-built housing, and the note must fix the two readings.

options.text: The two uses are identical, because housing and trade are one activity
options.misconception: merges two distinct economic activities into one concept

options.text: The word is neutral, so both uses describe legal arrangements in different words
options.misconception: treats a descriptive term as carrying no evaluative content

options.text: The word covers informal livelihoods and informal housing, which need different remedies
The word means only informal housing, so references to trading are mistranslations
options.misconception: reduces a two-sense word to a single sense without evidence

questions.explanation: The two uses name different phenomena: informal livelihoods concern trade and earnings, informal housing concern shelter and tenure. Conflating them hides the need for different responses.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two uses name the same problem.

questions.topic: Why a municipal finance reform fails to reach residents
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a decentralised reform produced no visible change on the ground

stimulus.body: The reform gave districts the power to set their own service charges within a band, and began publishing district budgets in a public register. Districts set low charges where local taxable income was weak, and few residents in those districts consulted the published register.

questions.stem: Translator's note F26: The passage describes a reform giving districts charging discretion, and the note must explain why residents saw little change.

options.text: Discretion failed because the band of permitted charges was set too narrow
options.misconception: blames the size of the charging band rather than its use

options.text: Publishing budgets was the failure, since transparency reduced what districts could raise
options.misconception: treats transparency as the cause of a failure to raise money

options.text: Reforms of this type always fail, so no partial success should be reported
options.misconception: generalises from one reform to a universal rule about reform

options.text: Discretion delivered to a district without income and without informed citizens changed little

questions.explanation: The reform gave discretion to a district lacking the income to charge more and an informed public to press for it, so the power went unused. Nothing supports a general claim that reforms never work.
questions.hint: Ask who could exercise the new power.

options.misconception: misstates how school planning draws on attendance records

options.text: Schools need no population data at all, since demand is fixed by law
options.misconception: assumes school demand is fixed and immune to change

questions.topic: Remittances and rural household spending
questions.learningObjective: Judge the net effect of rising remittances and falling local earnings
questions.stem: Translator's note H19: The passage describes a village where remittance income doubled while local agricultural earnings fell, and the note must convey the net effect.

options.text: The two changes are unrelated, because earnings and transfers move independently
options.misconception: assumes earnings and transfers never move apart

options.text: Households may be no poorer overall, but they have become more dependent on outside earnings
Households are clearly poorer, because remittances always fall short of local earnings lost
options.misconception: treats a fall in one income source as proof of poverty

options.text: Households are clearly better off, because external income removes all local risk
options.misconception: ignores the risk that comes with outside income

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Movement from city centre to its own region
questions.learningObjective: Explain the mechanism linking a population shift to service quality
questions.stem: Term note 6: The source links a population shift from the centre to the region with falling central service quality, and the note must set out the mechanism.

answer.exemplar: The centre built its networks for a denser and larger population, so when households move out, the same fixed assets serve fewer people while their maintenance cost per remaining user rises. The receiving region faces the mirror problem: new households on the edge require extensions that duplicate what the core already has. The shift therefore degrades service quality in the centre before it improves anything in the region.

questions.explanation: Assets sized for a larger core population are spread across fewer users after the shift, so upkeep per user rises and quality falls. The region must duplicate networks it lacks.
questions.hint: Ask how the cost per user changes.

questions.explanation: The added land value of 4,500,000 against a cost of 18,000,000 is one quarter, so the capture rate is 25 per cent. Whether that is sufficient depends on how much of the uplift the authority can tax.
questions.hint: Divide the added value by the cost.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Charging for peak road use
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a charge and a rebate work together on peak travel

stimulus.body: Drivers who charge their phone at a busy junction pay the congestion fee, and the money is returned to them as a discount on the same route in off-peak hours. The scheme was introduced to reduce the number of vehicles entering the centre in the morning peak.

questions.stem: Gloss entry 52: The passage describes a congestion charge with an off-peak rebate, and the note must convey how the two elements work together.

options.text: The scheme works by making the charge cheaper for those who drive most often
options.misconception: mistakes a deterrent for a reward for frequent driving

options.text: Because the fee is returned to the same drivers, the scheme has no effect on behaviour
options.misconception: ignores that the price signal changes when journeys are made

options.text: The charge deters peak entry while the rebate gives a reason to shift journeys to quieter hours
The rebate compensates drivers for charges they could not avoid at any time of day
options.misconception: misses that the rebate is targeted at off-peak travel

questions.explanation: Charging at the junction raises the cost of the peak journey while the rebate lowers the cost of moving it, so both push traffic to quieter hours. Returning money does not cancel the signal.
questions.hint: Ask where the price signal operates.

questions.stem: Translator's note K8: The passage reports that the district now supplies 46 per cent of households with a piped connection, and the note must convey what this means for the remainder.

options.text: With 46 per cent connected, the remaining households no longer need any water
options.misconception: assumes households outside the figure have no supply at all

options.text: The connection rate is the share of pipes installed, not of households supplied
options.misconception: confuses the share of households with the share of pipework

options.text: A 46 per cent connection rate means the network serves nearly every street
options.misconception: reads a household coverage rate as network coverage

options.text: Just over half of households still rely on standpipes, vendors or carried water for supply

questions.explanation: The complement of 46 per cent is 54 per cent, and those households must obtain water through standpipes, vendors or carrying. A connection rate measures households, not pipes.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a gap between approval rates for documented and undocumented applicants
questions.stem: Translator's note L14: The passage states that applications with documents were approved at 71 per cent while those without were approved at 12 per cent, and the note must convey the disparity.

options.text: Approval rates track documentation, so the procedure screens people by paperwork rather than need
Both rates are low enough that documentation makes no practical difference
options.misconception: understates a fifty-nine point gap between two rates

options.text: Twelve per cent approval for undocumented applicants shows the policy is applied evenly
options.misconception: reads a large disparity as evidence of uniform enforcement

options.text: The disparity proves that officials deliberately favour documented applicants
options.misconception: infers intent from an outcome difference with no evidence

questions.explanation: A 59 percentage point gap between the two groups shows the documentation rule is doing the screening work. The pattern demonstrates differential outcomes, but not deliberate intent.

questions.topic: Two readings of urban informality
questions.learningObjective: Weigh two readings of informality in a translation decision
questions.stem: Sense note 27: The translator must choose between reading informality as a survival strategy and reading it as a parallel economy, and the note must guide that choice.

options.text: The readings are stylistic, so the choice matters only for the tone of the text
options.misconception: reduces a choice of framing to a matter of literary style

options.text: The readings differ in emphasis, since one stresses necessity and the other a functioning system
The readings are exact opposites, so one of them must be false
options.misconception: treats two emphases as mutually exclusive truth claims

options.text: The readings are identical, since survival strategies always form parallel economies
options.misconception: assumes necessity and system formation are one phenomenon

questions.explanation: The two readings stress different aspects of one reality: how people cope and how the arrangements they create function. Choosing one does not make the other false.
questions.hint: Check whether the two readings can both hold.

options.text: Posting summaries online proves that residents were able to question the proposals
options.misconception: treats publication as evidence that residents engaged

options.text: The attendance figures show that residents rejected the reform at the meetings
options.misconception: confuses low attendance with active rejection of the reform

options.misconception: assumes a broadcast guarantees universal understanding

questions.explanation: Four of the six meetings drew no public questions, so the reform was mostly explained to officials rather than residents. Broadcasting and web posting widen reach but not understanding.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Movement from city centre to its own region
questions.learningObjective: Capture how a shift redistributes cost between the core and the region
questions.stem: Translator's note T39: The source explains how the centre's loss of residents affects the balance between the core and the wider region, and the note must capture the point.

answer.exemplar: The core and the region are affected by one movement in opposite directions. The core retains the fixed assets and the overheads of a larger city while serving a smaller population, so costs per remaining household rise. The region gains households and income but must extend the networks, clinics and schools that were designed for a smaller population. Neither side's interest alone describes the outcome of the shift.

questions.explanation: A single movement of residents creates losses for the core and costs for the region at the same time. Describing the change from one side alone therefore misrepresents what happened.
questions.hint: Look for the balance between the two areas.

options.text: The drop happened because recent arrivals needed less health care than other residents
options.misconception: explains an access drop by health need, not paperwork

options.text: Requiring documents usually increases registrations because it clarifies who is eligible
options.misconception: assumes a documentation rule always widens access

options.text: The drop shows that recent arrivals prefer private providers over public clinics

questions.learningObjective: Explain why documentary conditions can be regressive in effect
questions.stem: Translator's note AV58: The passage argues that documentary conditions for services are regressive in effect, and the note must set out the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: A documentary condition appears neutral because it applies the same rule to everyone, and that is precisely why it can be regressive in effect. The documents it demands are not held equally: recent arrivals, tenants without registration and households whose papers are held by other relatives are far less likely to have them. The rule therefore filters most sharply against the residents least able to absorb the consequences of losing a service.

questions.explanation: Uniform rules can bear unevenly when the documents they demand are held unevenly, and those least likely to hold them can least afford losing a service. That makes the effect regressive.

answer.exemplar: The first definition covers economic activity conducted outside the registration and licensing rules that the state applies, so that it escapes taxation and protection alike. options.text: Charging only at peak times makes the price reflect the scarce capacity of the road at that moment
Charging only at peak times is a revenue device aimed at infrequent visitors
options.misconception: treats congestion pricing as a simple revenue-raising device

options.text: Peak charging exists to discourage travel in the evenings rather than the mornings
options.misconception: reverses the time of day that the pricing targets

options.text: Peak charging is applied to make the charge easier to explain to drivers
options.misconception: explains a pricing design by administrative convenience

questions.explanation: The scarcity causing congestion exists only at peak times, so pricing only then makes the charge reflect the true cost of capacity used. It is a targeting principle, not a revenue measure.
questions.hint: Ask what the price is meant to reflect.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Share of residents with neither connection nor standpipe
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a connection rate leaves unsaid about supply reliability
questions.stem: Translator's note AK29: The passage reports that 71 per cent of households have a connection and asks what the remainder implies about the reliability of supply.

options.text: The unserved households are connected to the same piped network at a discounted tariff
options.misconception: assumes the unserved are connected at a discounted rate

options.text: For the remaining 29 per cent, supply depends on standpipes or vendors and can fail when those fail
With 71 per cent connected, the other households use private wells, which never fail
options.misconception: assumes an alternative supply route has no interruption risk

options.text: A connection rate of 71 per cent means each connected household receives nearly twice the average volume
options.misconception: turns a coverage rate into a statement about volume

questions.explanation: A connection rate reports who is connected, not how dependable their supply is, and the remaining 29 per cent draw on sources the authority cannot maintain. The share leaves reliability unmeasured.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when a standpipe runs dry.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Documentation as a condition of service
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a documentary condition can raise revenue while excluding some households
questions.stem: Sense note 46: The passage states that requiring a land title before a water connection raised revenue but also displaced households, and the note must convey both effects.

options.text: The requirement displaced households only because of a deliberate policy of exclusion
options.misconception: assumes displacement must have been a deliberate aim

options.text: The requirement had no distributional effect because it applied to all applicants equally
options.misconception: mistakes a uniform rule for a uniform effect on households

options.text: The requirement raises revenue from documented owners while excluding households whose tenure is informal
The requirement raised revenue because it removed households that never paid
options.misconception: attributes revenue gains to excluding non-paying households

questions.explanation: A title requirement changes who counts as an owner, so revenue can rise while informal tenure holders are excluded. A uniform rule can be selective because documents are not held equally.
questions.hint: Ask who holds the documents the rule needs.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Two readings of urban informality
questions.learningObjective: Identify which sense of informality fits a described settlement
questions.stem: Translator's note AH40: The passage describes settlements beside new formal housing and the translator must decide which sense of informality applies.

answer.exemplar: The description gives tenure and construction as the defining features, since the residents hold no secure title and the buildings carry no formal approval. Income, street naming and distance from the centre may all vary and are not what the passage marks as informal. A translation that selects the livelihood sense here would import a claim about employment that the passage never makes, and would obscure the legal status of the housing itself, which is the point the passage is making about service provision and secure tenure.

questions.explanation: The definition turns on tenure and construction, not on income, street naming or location. Choosing the livelihood sense would import a claim about employment that the passage never makes.
questions.hint: Point to what the passage says is missing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why a municipal finance reform fails to reach residents
questions.learningObjective: Pair a fiscal gain with weak reach in distant settlements

stimulus.body: The reform moved three functions from the district to the regional authority and raised the district's own-source revenue share from 18 to 41 per cent. Residents in settlements over twenty kilometres from the regional offices reported that they had not heard of the change, and no consultation meetings were held in those settlements.

questions.stem: Term note 52: The passage pairs a fiscal gain with weak reach in distant settlements, and the note must convey both.

options.text: The district lost autonomy, since transfers to the region always reduce local revenue
options.misconception: assumes transferring functions always lowers local revenue

options.text: Raising the local share to 41 per cent shows that no functions were transferred
options.misconception: confuses a rise in local revenue with cancelling a transfer

options.text: Residents in distant settlements opposed the reform at meetings that are not reported
options.misconception: invents opposition at meetings the passage never describes

options.text: The district gained revenue autonomy while distant residents received neither consultation nor notice

questions.explanation: The two facts describe a reform that succeeded for the budget and failed for reach: the local share rose to 41 per cent, yet distant settlements were neither consulted nor informed.
questions.hint: Notice what the settlement figures cannot show.
